# Evaluation in Production {#sec-production-eval}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One measurement, designed to answer a question the
book has not yet asked: how far does an eval score move when *nothing* changed?
A 100-item Turkish extraction suite with ground truth known by construction, run
five times each under three prompts — the one that shipped, one with a rule
deleted, and one with the same rules merely reordered. @sec-llm-eval sized an
eval set; this chapter measures the noise floor of the gate that reads it.
Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `qwen2.5:7b`, Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- place a change on the ladder from offline eval to A/B test, and say what each
  rung catches and what it cannot;
- measure your own gate's noise floor before trusting any score it reports;
- design a gate threshold that blocks regressions without blocking noise;
- recognise that a cosmetically identical prompt edit is not a cosmetically
  identical change;
- curate a golden set from real traffic, and know when it has aged out;
- score a sample of live traffic without scoring all of it;
- treat user feedback as the biased sample it is, and size an A/B test before
  running it;
- separate the three kinds of drift that look the same on a dashboard.

## The ladder, and what each rung can catch {#sec-production-eval-ladder}

Everything up to now evaluated systems in a room by themselves. Production adds
a constraint that changes the whole design: [the thing you are evaluating is
already serving users while you evaluate it]{.hl}. That turns evaluation from a
single event into a ladder. The table lists the rungs from the cheapest to the
most expensive, and each rung sees less than the one after it.

| rung | what it costs | what it catches | what it cannot see |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Offline eval** | seconds, no users | regressions on cases you thought of | anything your suite does not contain |
| **CI gate** | one build | a bad change *before* merge | whether the change helps real users |
| **Shadow** | double inference, no user impact | crashes, latency, malformed output on live inputs | the *effect on users* — nobody is served the output, so nothing about behaviour, satisfaction or downstream action is observable |
| **Canary** | a slice of real users | quality failures, while a failure still reaches only a few users (@sec-deployment) | small effects — the slice is too small to resolve them |
| **A/B test** | days, and real exposure | whether it actually helps | fast-moving regressions — unless you wire in guardrail metrics and a stopping rule, which you should; an A/B test is not a commitment to run it out |

: Five rungs, in the order a change should climb them {tbl-colwidths="[14,20,33,33]"}

Four of the rung names are engineering jargon. **CI** (continuous integration)
is the set of automated checks that runs on every proposed change to the code
before that change is *merged* into the main version; a **CI gate** is a check
that can refuse the merge. In a **shadow** deployment the new version receives a
copy of live requests, but its answers are only stored, never shown to users. A
**canary** serves the new version to a small share of real users first, so a
failure is seen early and rolled back (@sec-deployment-release covers both). An
**A/B test** splits users at random
between the old version (A) and the new one (B) and compares outcomes;
@sec-production-eval-ab sizes one.

The mistake is not skipping a rung. It is *believing* a rung about something it
cannot see. A shadow deployment that runs clean tells you the new prompt does
not crash; on its own it says nothing about whether the answers are worse,
because nobody looked at one. That last part is a choice, not a limit of the
method: shadow outputs are stored, and you can score them afterwards against a
reference, with a validated judge, or by reading a sample. What shadow can never
give you is how users would have *responded* to them. A green CI gate tells you the change did not regress the cases
in your suite, which is a claim about your suite.

This chapter is mostly about the second rung, because it is the one teams get
wrong in a specific and measurable way.

## A prompt change is a code change {#sec-production-eval-ci}

A prompt is the single highest-leverage, least-reviewed artefact in an LLM
system. It is a text file; it changes behaviour more than most refactors; and it
is routinely edited on a branch, skimmed in review, and merged on the strength
of "reads fine to me".

The discipline that fixes this is borrowed wholesale from testing:

1. **The suite lives in the repository**, next to the prompt it exercises, and
   moves with it.
2. **The gate runs on every change to the prompt**, not on a schedule and not
   when someone remembers.
3. **The gate blocks the merge**, or it is not a gate — it is a dashboard, and
   dashboards do not stop anything.
4. **A production failure becomes a case in the suite** before the fix is
   merged — and you confirm that the case fails before the fix and passes after
   it — which is @sec-agent-eval's regression discipline applied to prompts.

All of that is standard practice imported from software engineering, and none of
it is the hard part. [The hard part is that an eval score is a random variable
and a unit test is not.]{.hl} `assert add(2, 2) == 4` returns the same answer
every time. A suite score does not, and a gate built as though it does will
either block changes at random or wave regressions through. Which of those you
get depends on a number almost nobody measures: how much the score moves when
nothing changed.

## What the gate can actually see {#sec-production-eval-noise}

So measure it. The suite is 100 Turkish customer messages generated from five
templates with randomised slots — order code, day, month, city, amount — which
means the ground truth is known by construction rather than by hand labelling,
and there is no annotation error to argue about. The task is extraction to JSON:
five fields per message, 500 field decisions per run. Scoring is exact string
match per field, plus a stricter all-five-correct **exact match** per item.

Three prompts, all extracting the same five fields:

- **A — the one that shipped.** Six rules: one on output format, then one per
  field, in the order the fields are listed.
- **B — a rule deleted.** Identical to A with the `city` rule removed. This is
  the regression a reviewer waves through, and it is here as a control that the
  measurement can detect *something*.
- **C — the same rules reordered.** Byte-for-byte the same six rules as A,
  listed in reverse. No rule added, none removed, no wording changed. This is
  the edit that gets approved without comment.

Each prompt ran the full 100-item suite five times at temperature 0.7, and A ran
twice more at temperature 0.

### The noise floor is smaller than folklore claims

Prompt A, five identical runs of the same suite against the same model:

```text
prompt A, temp 0.7, five runs
  field accuracy   95.4  95.4  95.6  95.8  96.0     mean 95.64   sd 0.26
  exact match      80    81    81    82    82       mean 81.20   sd 0.84
```

[The worst pair of identical runs differs by 0.60 points of field accuracy.]{.hl}
That is an *estimate* of the noise floor, and it is worth being precise about
what it is not: a bound. The range of five draws is not a ceiling on the sixth.
Two fresh runs exceed 0.60 points about **10%** of the time at this `sd`, and
the expected widest gap across fifty runs — which is what a CI gate accumulates
in a couple of months — is **1.17** points rather than 0.60. Five runs are also
barely enough to estimate a standard deviation at all: the $\chi^2$ interval on
$\sigma$ from four degrees of freedom runs from 0.16 to 0.75, a factor of 4.8.

So write down `sd = 0.26`, not the range, because `sd` is the quantity that
scales. The floor is still small — small enough that the common objection to
eval gates, that LLM scores are too noisy to gate on, is simply not true for a
suite of this size and a task of this shape.
It is worth measuring rather than assuming, in both directions: folklore
overstates it here, and will understate it on a harder task with a judge in the
loop (in @sec-llm-eval a small judge flipped its verdict on 38% of items when
the candidates' order was swapped).

### The deleted rule is trivially visible

Prompt B, the missing `city` rule, against A:

```text
                    A       B      delta
  field accuracy   95.64   79.80   -15.84 pt   = 26x the noise floor
  exact match      81.20   21.40   -59.80 pt   = 30x the noise floor

  per field (of 100)      A      B
    order_id             100    100
    day                   91     86
    month                 99     98
    city                 100     29     <-- the deleted rule
    amount                88     86
```

No subtlety here, and that is the point of including it: a change that removes a
rule is 26 times the noise floor and is caught by any gate at all. If this were
the only kind of regression, gate design would not be interesting.

### The cosmetic edit is not cosmetic

Prompt C reorders the same six rules and changes nothing else.

```text
                    A       C      delta
  field accuracy   95.64   92.24   -3.40 pt   = 5.7x the noise floor
  exact match      81.20   72.00   -9.20 pt   = 4.6x the noise floor

  per field (of 100)      A      C
    order_id             100    100
    day                   91     74     <-- the entire regression
    month                 99     99
    city                 100     99
    amount                88     89
```

[Reordering six rules that were not otherwise touched cost 3.4 points of field
accuracy and 9.2 points of exact match, concentrated almost entirely in one
field.]{.hl} The reason this is easy to wave through is that the diff contains
no new text: every line already existed and only their order moved, which is the
one kind of change a reviewer has no content to react to. The rules are the same
rules.

**Which of those two numbers survives a test, and which does not.** Both
prompts ran the same 100 items, so the comparison is paired, and the per-item
pairings were not stored — but the margins (the two totals, 91 and 74) bound
the answer. A *discordant* item is one where the two prompts disagree: right
under one, wrong under the other. On the `day` field, 91 correct under A against
74 under C leaves a net 17 discordant decisions in one direction, and across
*every* split consistent with those margins McNemar's exact test (the paired
test of @sec-llm-eval, which looks only at discordant items) gives p between 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ and 0.006. That
regression is real on any reading. The exact-match difference does not fare as
well: 81 against 72 leaves a net 9, and the same sweep gives p anywhere from
0.004 to 0.24, so it can be significant or nothing at all depending on
pairings nobody wrote down. Store the per-item results, which costs nothing and
is the difference between a claim and an anecdote.

::: {.column-margin}
This is why "prompt engineering" resists being called engineering: the artefact
has no interface, so no edit can be proven local. Ordering is load-bearing and
invisible.
:::

The failure mode is specific enough to name. A separate probe took 40 items,
ran them under each prompt, and inspected every wrong `day` value:

```text
  prompt A:  day wrong on  4/40 — 4 of 4  are the leading digits of the amount
  prompt C:  day wrong on 13/40 — 13 of 13 are the leading digits of the amount

    want day 18   got  6   amount   6.842,50
    want day 12   got  1   amount   1.289,50
    want day 26   got  5   amount   5.669,99
    want day  8   got 29   amount     290,50
```

**In that probe every single wrong `day`, under both prompts, is the leading
digits of the amount.** The model bleeds one field into another, and moving the `amount` rule
above the `day` rule roughly triples how often it does. The bug was always
there — prompt A has it at 10% — and the reorder amplified it.

That is a much more useful finding than "reordering is risky". It says the
regression had a mechanism, the mechanism was visible in the per-field
breakdown, and a suite that reported only an aggregate score would have shown a
3.4-point wobble with no way to tell whether it mattered. Report per-field
or per-category numbers or you will not be able to act on the aggregate.

### Temperature 0 buys reproducibility, not correctness

Prompt A, twice at temperature 0:

```text
  field accuracy   95.20   95.20      per-item results byte-identical
  exact match      80      80
```

Perfectly reproducible: not merely the same score, but the same result on every
one of the 100 items. That is worth having in a gate, because it removes the
run-to-run noise and makes a failing run reproducible on a laptop.

Two caveats, both worth stating. Temperature 0 scored **95.20**, which sits
*below* the entire temperature-0.7 range of 95.40–96.00 — greedy decoding is one
particular sample, not the best one. And it does not fix anything: the
leading-digit bug survives greedy decoding, which scored `day` 90/100 with 8 of
its 10 misses being the same amount-bleed. Determinism
makes a gate reproducible; it does not make it right. Your users are
probably not served at temperature 0 either, so a temperature-0 gate measures a
configuration you do not ship.

Two further limits keep "no noise" from meaning "every delta is real". First,
the byte-identical result is a property of this setup — one local server
answering one request at a time. Hosted APIs and servers that batch many
requests together often return slightly different text at temperature 0, so
check it on yours, as @sec-decoding also recommends. Second, any
prompt edit, even one that changes no meaning, flips the greedy output on a few
items. A small delta between two temperature-0 runs of *different* prompts can
therefore still be chance, and it still needs the paired test above.

## Designing the gate so it fires on the right things {#sec-production-eval-gate}

Given a noise floor, a gate is a threshold decision, and the obvious threshold is
wrong in an instructive way. To see how a threshold behaves, the measured
per-item results were resampled 2,000 times per cell of the tables below. Each
draw compares one baseline run against one new run, as a real gate does, and
the tables report how often the gate fired. One caveat on provenance: the per-item pairing across variants was not
stored (see above), so this resampling cannot have been item-matched across A
and C. Read the rates below as an illustration of how a threshold behaves, not
as measured operating characteristics of a paired gate.

| suite size | naive gate: A vs A **(false block)** | A vs B (caught) | A vs C (caught) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 20 | 22.9% | 100% | 93.0% |
| 50 | 35.6% | 100% | 99.6% |
| 100 | 42.5% | 100% | 100% |

: A gate that blocks whenever the new score is lower {tbl-colwidths="[16,30,27,27]"}

The naive gate — block if the new run scores lower than the baseline — catches
almost every regression, and [blocks 42.5% of changes that changed nothing]{.hl}. Worse, it
gets *worse as the suite grows*: at 20 items the two runs often tie exactly, and
ties pass; at 100 items exact ties are rare, so the comparison converges on a
coin flip. A team that responds to a flaky gate by adding more test cases makes
it flakier.

In this resampling experiment, a one-point threshold reduced the false-block
rate:

| suite size | 1-point threshold: A vs A **(false block)** | A vs B (caught) | A vs C (caught) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 20 | 20.5% | 100% | 90.8% |
| 50 | 6.6% | 100% | 96.2% |
| 100 | 4.3% | 100% | 99.4% |

: Block only if the new score is more than one point lower
{tbl-colwidths="[16,30,27,27]"}

At 100 items the gate blocks 4.3% of no-op changes and still catches the
reordered prompt 99.4% of the time. Now the suite size helps, as it should. The
rule that generalises:

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Signal against the noise floor, field accuracy</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 760 250" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart comparing the eval gate noise floor of 0.6 points against a 3.4 point regression from reordering prompt rules and a 15.84 point regression from deleting a rule">
  <text x="8" y="16" class="t-xs t-muted t-b">MEASURED ON 100 ITEMS, FIVE RUNS PER PROMPT</text>

  <text x="8" y="48" class="t-xs t-b">noise floor</text>
  <text x="8" y="64" class="t-xs t-muted">same prompt, two runs</text>
  <rect x="200" y="36" width="18" height="26" rx="3" class="box"/>
  <text x="228" y="55" class="t-sm t-mono">0.60 pt</text>

  <text x="8" y="106" class="t-xs t-b t-accent">rules reordered</text>
  <text x="8" y="122" class="t-xs t-muted">nothing added or removed</text>
  <rect x="200" y="94" width="102" height="26" rx="3" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="312" y="113" class="t-sm t-mono">3.40 pt &#183; 5.7x noise</text>

  <text x="8" y="164" class="t-xs t-b">one rule deleted</text>
  <text x="8" y="180" class="t-xs t-muted">the obvious regression</text>
  <rect x="200" y="152" width="475" height="26" rx="3" class="box"/>
  <text x="200" y="200" class="t-sm t-mono">15.84 pt &#183; 26x noise</text>

  <path d="M8,216 H752" class="ln-thin"/>
  <text x="8" y="238" class="t-xs t-muted">A gate with a 1-point threshold sees both regressions and blocks 4.3% of no-op changes. A gate with no threshold blocks 42.5% of them.</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.fig-cap}
The deleted rule is not the interesting case. The reordered prompt is: a diff
whose every line is a line that was already there, nearly six times the five-run
range, and entirely inside one field.
:::
::::

**Set the threshold from your measured noise floor, with headroom.** Run your
suite against an unchanged system five times and record the run-to-run `sd` —
not the range, which is a five-draw estimate that future runs will exceed. A
threshold placed just above the observed range barely helps: at this `sd` two
fresh runs clear 0.60 points a tenth of the time. Roughly **4 × `sd`** is the
working rule, which here is the 1.0-point threshold used above.

The headroom is large because `sd` itself is uncertain. If the five-run `sd`
were exact, the difference between two runs would have a standard deviation of
$\sqrt{2}\times$`sd`, and a threshold of $k \times$ `sd` would falsely block
about $\Phi(-k/\sqrt{2})$ of no-op changes ($\Phi$ is the standard normal
cumulative distribution): roughly 8% at 2 × `sd`, 2% at 3 × `sd` and 0.2% at
4 × `sd`. The resampling above found 4.3% at 1.0 point — twenty times that 0.2%.
It behaves as if the true run-to-run `sd` were nearer 0.45 than 0.26. (Solving
the formula for 4.3% gives about 0.45 once you account for scores moving in
0.2-point steps, so "more than one point lower" means at least 1.2 points; ignoring
that discreteness gives about 0.41.) Either value is well inside the $\chi^2$
interval of 0.16 to 0.75. Four times a five-run
estimate is what keeps false blocks at a few percent even when the estimate
came out low. That is a twenty-minute experiment that turns a gate
people learn to ignore into one they trust. A gate that is overridden by habit
is worse than no gate, because the record then shows a green check where a
human actually skipped the test.

## The golden set has a lifecycle {#sec-production-eval-golden}

The suite above was generated, which is honest for measuring a noise floor and
useful for exactly the capabilities its templates define — and not
representative of production quality, because it contains exactly the phenomena
those templates contain and nothing else. A real golden set comes from real traffic, and it is not a static
artefact.

**It is born from failures.** The first entries should be things that actually
broke. @sec-observability's traces are the raw material: the run someone
complained about is a scenario with its inputs already recorded.

**It must be sampled deliberately, not conveniently.** Traffic is
heavy-tailed, so uniform sampling gives you a hundred variations of the most
common request. Stratify — by intent, by length, by language, by customer
segment — and deliberately oversample the rare and the hard, or the set will be
easy in exactly the way production is not.

**It carries personal data, and that is a decision.** Real traffic contains real
customers. @sec-observability's redaction argument applies, and pseudonymising
before the set enters the repository is the only place it can be done once;
@sec-governance covers the obligations. A golden set is a copy of production
data with a long retention period, which is precisely the thing your policy is
about.

**It ages, and the failure is silent.** Two mechanisms. The set gets *easier* as
you fix the things in it, so a stable score means less each quarter — the same
saturation @sec-llm-eval described for public benchmarks, arriving in your own
repository. And the traffic moves out from under it: users find new phrasings,
the product ships new features, and the set describes last year's product.
[A golden set that has not changed in six months is not stable, it is
stale.]{.hl} Budget refresh as routine work: add items from recent failures and
record when each item entered. Retire items nothing fails any more, but only
from the part of the set sampled to represent current traffic; items that
entered as real failures are regression tests, and they stay.

**Its size is set by @sec-llm-eval's arithmetic, not by taste.** That chapter
measured it: at 80% power on a system that is right 80% of the time, 30 items
detect nothing at all, 100 items detect 13.4 points, and 1,000 detect 4.8.
Those figures belong to an 80% baseline, so redo the arithmetic for your own
metric rather than borrowing them. Exact match here sits at 81%, close to that
baseline, and the reordered prompt cost it 9.2 points — *less* than the 13.4
points that 100 items per system can resolve without pairing. Field accuracy is
a different case: near 96% the binomial variance $p(1-p)$ is about a quarter of
its value at 80%. This suite has 500 field decisions per run, and the same
calculation says 500 unpaired decisions per system resolve a drop from 95.6% of
only about 4.4 points (1,000 would bring that down to about 2.9). The reorder's
3.4-point drop sits *below* that. Yet the gate on these same 100
items fires on the reordered prompt 99.4% of the time.

Those two numbers answer different questions, and it is worth keeping them
apart. The 13.4 and 4.8 are **minimum detectable effects**: they carry the
uncertainty of estimating an unknown effect from a fresh sample. The 99.4% is
an **operating characteristic of a decision rule**: given these fixed 100 items
and this measured difference in means, how often does the threshold trip? It
conditions on the observed 3.40 being the true effect, so it is not power and
does not generalise past this suite. Both are worth reporting — the gate's
false-block and catch rates for operations, the paired test above for the claim
that the regression is real. Pairing is what makes the second possible at this
sample size, which is why a gate compares runs on identical items rather than
on fresh samples.

## Scoring live traffic without scoring all of it {#sec-production-eval-online}

Offline evaluation asks whether the system handles cases you collected. Online
evaluation asks whether it is handling the cases arriving right now. You cannot
score all of them — with a judge about as large as the model it judges, judging
every request roughly doubles inference cost — so the question is what to
sample.

The cheap signals first, because they need no judge and cover all traffic:
schema validity and parse rate (@sec-decoding), refusal rate, latency and token
counts (@sec-observability), tool error rate, retry rate, and truncation at the
step ceiling (@sec-deployment). None of these tell you whether an answer was
good, and all of them move sharply when something has broken.

Then a judge, on a sample, with three things sampled together:

- **a small uniform slice** — a fixed percentage, so the baseline is comparable
  over time;
- **everything that already looks wrong** — errors, retries, ceiling hits,
  thumbs-down, escalations;
- **a stratified slice of the rare cases** you would otherwise never see.

Two disciplines make the number usable. **Audit the online judge exactly as
@sec-llm-eval audits an offline one** — it is the same instrument with less
supervision, and a judge that flips on 38% of items when you swap the order will
do so in production too. And **record the judge's version and prompt alongside
the score**, because a judge upgrade shifts the whole series; @sec-gateway's
pinning argument applies to the evaluator as much as to the model.

## User feedback and A/B tests {#sec-production-eval-ab}

Two more kinds of evidence exist only in production: what users tell you, and
what they do when you change the system under them.

**User feedback is a biased sample, not a metric.** Explicit signals — a
thumbs-up or thumbs-down, a star rating, a written complaint — come from a small
minority of users, and not a random one: people who are annoyed, or delighted,
rate more often than people who simply got their answer and left. That is
selection bias, and it means a thumbs-down *rate* describes the users who chose
to click, not your traffic. Implicit signals — the user regenerates the answer,
copies it, edits it, asks the same question again, abandons the conversation or
asks for a human — cover everyone, but each is a proxy with more than one
meaning: a regenerate can mean "wrong" or "show me another version". A
thumbs-down also mixes "wrong" with "not what I wanted": a correct refusal, or
an accurate answer the user did not like, collects one too. Optimise a system
directly for thumbs-up and you meet @sec-post-training's reward hacking again:
answers that please rise, answers that are right but unwelcome fall. And the
rate moves when the interface moves — a button that is easier to reach changes
the rate with no change in quality. So use feedback the way the previous
section does: as a *sampler* that sends suspicious cases to the judge and to
people, and as a source of golden-set candidates — not as the quality score.

**An A/B test answers the question the other rungs leave open**: does the change
help real users? It is the only rung that can, because random assignment makes
the two groups alike in everything except the version they received. Four
decisions are written down *before* it starts:

1. **The unit of randomisation.** Usually the user, not the request, so one
   person does not meet two behaviours in one conversation. Analyse at the same
   level: one user's requests are correlated, so treating 50,000 requests from
   5,000 users as 50,000 independent observations overstates your precision.
2. **One primary metric** — the outcome the change is meant to move, such as
   the share of conversations resolved without a human. Choosing it after
   seeing the data is the many-tests problem @sec-llm-eval warns about: check
   enough metrics and one of them crosses p < 0.05 by chance.
3. **Guardrail metrics** — what must *not* get worse while you pursue the
   primary one: latency, cost per conversation, escalation rate, complaint rate.
   The name is A/B-testing vocabulary, not the runtime guardrail of
   @sec-guardrails, although a clearly breached guardrail metric should stop
   the test just as fast.
4. **The sample size and the stopping rule.**

The sample size is @sec-llm-eval's arithmetic again, but real effects on user
outcomes are small, so the numbers become large. For two independent groups,
detecting a change from $p_1$ to $p_2$ at 80% power and a two-sided 5% level
needs about

$$
n \approx \frac{(1.96 + 0.84)^2 \,\bigl[p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)\bigr]}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}
$$

users *per arm*. If 20% of conversations now end in an escalation to a human
and you hope to cut that to 18%, that is about 6,000 users per arm; to detect a
one-point change, from 20% to 19%, about 24,600 per arm. [Halving the effect you
want to see multiplies the sample by about four]{.hl}, because the difference
sits squared in the denominator. At 5,000 eligible users a day split evenly,
the one-point test needs about ten days — which is why the A/B test is the slow
rung.

The stopping rule matters as much as the size. Checking the p-value every day
and stopping at the first p < 0.05 — *peeking* — inflates the false-positive
rate far beyond 5%: in a simulation of an A/A test (both arms identical) with
ten equally spaced looks, about 19% of runs crossed the line at some look. Fix
the duration in advance and test once at the end, or use a sequential test
designed for repeated looks. Guardrail metrics are watched continuously for the
opposite reason: stopping early for harm is cheap, while a false *win* ships.
And before the first real test, run an A/A test through the whole pipeline — it
is this chapter's noise-floor measurement, applied to the experiment platform.

## Three kinds of drift that look identical on a dashboard {#sec-production-eval-drift}

A quality metric declines. The dashboard shows one line going down, and there
are three unrelated causes with three unrelated fixes.

| what moved | what it looks like | how to tell | what to do |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **The model** | a step change on a specific day, across all traffic | `gen_ai.response.model` changed while `gen_ai.request.model` did not (@sec-observability) | pin versions (@sec-gateway); re-run the golden set against both |
| **The inputs** | a gradual slide, concentrated in some segments | input distribution moved: new phrasings, lengths, languages, a new customer | refresh the golden set; the system did not change, the job did |
| **The system** | a step change you can attribute to a deploy | it lines up with a release (@sec-deployment) | the gate should have caught it; add the case that escaped |

: Same line, three causes {tbl-colwidths="[14,28,32,26]"}

[Recording the responded model and the input distribution is what separates
these; without them, all three are "quality is down" and the response is a
guess.]{.hl} The distinguishing evidence is cheap and must be collected in
advance — you cannot reconstruct last month's input distribution after the fact.

How do you *see* the inputs move? Compare recent traffic with a reference window
on a few cheap descriptors: input length, language, the share of each intent
(from a classifier, or from clusters of input embeddings as in @sec-clustering),
and the share of inputs that sit far from every golden-set item in embedding
space. A chi-square test on the binned counts, or simply a chart of the shares
over time, shows which segment has grown; the last descriptor also points to the
new inputs your golden set does not cover.

A fourth case deserves naming because it is often the most common: nothing
drifted, and your metric is noisy. That is what the noise floor is for. A weekly
re-run of a fixed suite that moves 0.5 points is not a signal on a suite whose
measured floor is 0.6. An online score has a larger floor still, because each
week it is computed on *different* requests: on top of run-to-run noise it
carries ordinary sampling error. For a judged sample of 500 requests with an
80% pass rate that is a standard error of about 1.8 points — compute it before
you read a weekly wobble as drift.

## Routing the uncertain cases to people {#sec-production-eval-humans}

Automated scoring runs out where it matters most: the cases where the system is
unsure, the judge is unreliable, or the cost of being wrong is high. Those go to
people, and the pipeline is @sec-data-annotation's, pointed at production.

What makes it work is that routing is a *policy*, written down and measured, not
a queue somebody watches. Three inputs decide it: model uncertainty where you
have it, disagreement between judges or between a judge and a rule, and
stakes — a refund, a medical claim and a shipping query do not deserve the same
scrutiny. @sec-guardrails is where the enforcement side of that policy lives.

The output of human review is not one artefact but three, and teams routinely
capture only the first: the immediate decision on that case; a labelled item for
the golden set; and, when the same failure appears a third time, a change to the
system rather than a third correction. [If human review produces only decisions,
you have bought a manual process, not a feedback loop.]{.hl}

The cost model that follows is worth stating plainly, because it is what makes
the case to a budget-holder: review capacity is fixed, so the question is never
"should humans check this" but "which slice of traffic do the humans we have
look at". That makes routing a resource-allocation problem with an obvious
objective — send them the cases where their judgement changes an outcome.

## The loop this part builds toward {#sec-production-eval-loop}

Every chapter in this part has been one arc of the same loop, and it is worth
seeing assembled:

1. **Serve it** (@sec-serving) and **route it** (@sec-gateway).
2. **Deploy it so failure is survivable** (@sec-deployment).
3. **Instrument it** (@sec-observability), so a complaint reaches a span.
4. **Turn that span into a test** — this chapter, and @sec-agent-eval's
   discipline.
5. **Gate the next change on the test**, with a threshold set from a measured
   noise floor.
6. **Sample live traffic** to find the failures nobody reported.
7. **Route the uncertain ones to people**, and feed their labels back to step 4.

The loop is not exotic. It is the operational rhythm of any mature software
system, with two adjustments for this setting: the tests are statistical rather
than deterministic, and the artefact under test is a text file that nobody
thinks of as code.

## Intuition checks {#sec-production-eval-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. The first three carry the chapter's
measurements — the noise floor, the cosmetic edit that was not cosmetic, and the
gate that gets worse as it grows. The last three are about what a green gate
does and does not license you to believe.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Are LLM eval scores too noisy to gate a merge on?

Measure it before believing either answer. Here they were not.

The same prompt, run five times over the same 100-item suite, gave `sd = 0.26`
and spanned 0.60 points of field accuracy. That is the noise floor, and it is
small enough to gate on — but set the threshold from the `sd` with headroom
rather than from the range, because the range of five draws is an estimate the
sixth run will sometimes beat. About 4 × `sd` is the working rule.

The number is task-specific and will be larger with a judge in the loop
(in @sec-llm-eval a small judge flipped on 38% of items when the order was
swapped) or a smaller suite. The
transferable part is not 0.26; it is that a twenty-minute experiment — run the
unchanged system five times, record the spread — replaces an argument with a
threshold.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. A colleague reorders the rules in a prompt. Same rules, same words. Safe?

No, and this is the chapter's central measurement.

Reordering six rules — none added, none removed, no wording changed — cost
**3.40 points of field accuracy and 9.20 points of exact match**. Name the
denominator when you quote a multiple: that is roughly six times the five-run
*range* of 0.60 points, and about thirteen times the run-to-run `sd` of 0.26.
Every "× noise" figure in this chapter is against the range, because that is
what a reader compares a single new run to; `sd` is the number to build the
threshold from. The whole regression sat in one field: `day` fell from 91
to 74 out of 100.

The mechanism is nameable. Across a 40-item probe, every wrong `day` under both
prompts was the leading digits of the *amount* — the model bleeds one field into another, and
moving the `amount` rule above the `day` rule tripled how often it did. The bug
existed in the shipped prompt at 10%; the reorder amplified it.

A prompt has no interface, so no edit to it is provably local. That is the
argument for gating prompt changes at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your eval gate is flaky. Should you add more test cases?

Not on its own — with a naive gate, more cases make it flakier.

Measured: a gate that blocks whenever the new score is lower falsely blocks
**22.9%** of no-op changes at 20 items, **35.6%** at 50, and **42.5%** at 100. At
small sizes the two runs often tie exactly and ties pass; as the suite grows,
exact ties disappear and the comparison converges on a coin flip.

Add a threshold first. At one point and 100 items, false blocks fall to **4.3%**
while the reordered prompt is still caught **99.4%** of the time — and now the
extra cases help, as you expected them to. Set the threshold from your measured
noise floor rather than from a round number.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Should the gate run at temperature 0?

It is a real benefit with two real limits.

At temperature 0 the two runs here were byte-identical per item — not just the
same score, the same result on all 100. That removes the run-to-run noise on
this setup (batched or hosted serving may not be as exact) and makes a failing
gate reproducible on a laptop, which is worth a lot.

But greedy decoding scored **95.20**, *below* the entire temperature-0.7 range of
95.40–96.00: it is one particular sample, not the best one. And it fixed nothing
— the leading-digit bug was still there. You also probably do not serve users at
temperature 0, so the gate measures a configuration you do not ship.

Reasonable resolution: gate at temperature 0 for reproducibility, and separately
track the sampled configuration you actually serve.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Your golden set's score has been flat for six months. Good news?

Almost certainly not — it is the most common way an eval program dies quietly.

Two things happen at once. The set gets easier as you fix what is in it, so a
flat score reflects a solved set rather than a healthy system: @sec-llm-eval's
benchmark saturation, arriving in your own repository. And traffic moves out from
under it — new phrasings, new features, new customers — so the set describes last
year's product.

A stale set is worse than no set, because it produces a green check. Keep two
sets rather than one: a **regression** set that only ever grows, where an item
earned its place by once being a real failure and stays forever precisely so an
old bug cannot return unnoticed, and a **representative** set sampled from
current traffic and refreshed on a schedule. Retiring items nothing fails is
right for the second and wrong for the first. Record when each item entered,
and treat refresh as routine work rather than a project.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Quality is down 4 points this month. What broke?

Four candidates, and you cannot distinguish them after the fact without evidence
collected in advance.

**The model moved** — a step change on one day, visible as
`gen_ai.response.model` changing while `gen_ai.request.model` did not
(@sec-observability). **The inputs moved** — a gradual slide in some segments;
the system is unchanged and the job is not. **The system moved** — a step change
that lines up with a deploy, and a case your gate did not contain. **Or nothing
moved** and the metric is noisy.

Rule out the fourth first, using the noise floor. Then the responded model and
the input distribution separate the other three — both cheap, and both impossible
to reconstruct retrospectively.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-production-eval-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurement makes answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the problem

**Q: How is evaluating an LLM system in CI different from running unit tests?**

The assertion is statistical rather than deterministic. A unit test returns the
same answer every run; a suite score is a random variable, so a gate needs a
threshold and the threshold needs a measured noise floor. Say how you would get
one: run the unchanged system five times over the same suite and record the
run-to-run `sd`, not only the widest gap. Measured here on 100 items that was
`sd = 0.26` points, with an observed range of 0.60 — small enough to gate on,
which is the opposite of the usual assumption. The threshold goes at roughly
4 × `sd`, because later runs will exceed a five-run range.

**Q: A change to a prompt only reorders existing instructions. Does it need an
eval run?**

Yes, and this is the case that convinces people. Reordering six rules with no
other edit cost 3.4 points of field accuracy and 9.2 of exact match here — about
six times the noise floor — with the entire regression inside one field. A prompt
has no interface, so no edit is provably local, and a reviewer has no way to
tell a cosmetic prompt change from a behavioural one by reading it.

**Q: How would you size a golden set?**

From the difference you need to detect, using @sec-llm-eval's arithmetic: at 80%
power on an 80%-accurate system, 100 items resolves 13.4 points and 1,000
resolves 4.8 — and redo that for your own baseline, because near 96% accuracy
the variance is about four times smaller. Then note the distinction that matters for gating — those are
unpaired minimum detectable effects, and a gate compares two runs on the *same*
items. Do not cite the 99.4% catch rate as evidence for pairing: the resampling
behind it could not match items across prompts, and it takes the observed
3.4-point drop as the true effect, so it illustrates a threshold rather than
measuring a paired gate. What pairing does buy is a test on the same items:
McNemar's test finds the `day` regression real on every pairing consistent with
the margins, and only stored per-item results would settle the exact-match
difference.

### Testing whether you have run one

**Q: Your eval gate blocks good changes and people started overriding it. Fix
it.**

First diagnose rather than loosen it: the usual cause is a gate with no
threshold, which measured here falsely blocks 42.5% of no-op changes at 100
items — and gets worse as the suite grows, because exact ties become rare. Set a
threshold from the measured noise floor; at one point that fell to 4.3% while
still catching a real regression 99.4% of the time. Then say why it is urgent:
a habitually overridden gate is worse than none, because the override is recorded
as a green check.

**Q: Offline evals are green and users are complaining. What do you do?**

Accept that the suite is the hypothesis being falsified. Go to traces
(@sec-observability), find the complained-about runs, and check whether the
failure class exists in the suite at all — usually it does not, which is a
curation problem rather than a scoring one. Add those cases, then ask why they
were absent: convenience sampling from a heavy-tailed distribution, or a set that
has aged out. Also check the fourth possibility — that the offline metric is
measuring something users do not care about.

**Q: How much production traffic would you score with an LLM judge, and which?**

Not all of it: with a judge of similar size, judging every request roughly
doubles inference cost. Take the
free signals on 100% — parse rate, refusals, latency, tool errors, ceiling hits —
then judge three overlapping samples: a fixed uniform slice for a comparable
baseline, everything that already looks wrong, and a stratified slice of rare
cases. Then the two disciplines: audit the online judge the way you would an
offline one, and pin and record its version, because a judge upgrade shifts the
entire series.

**Q: Product wants the thumbs-down rate as the headline quality metric. What do
you say?**

That it is a biased sample, not a measurement. Only a small, self-selected
minority clicks; a thumbs-down mixes "wrong" with "unwelcome"; and the rate
moves with the interface. Optimising it rewards pleasing answers over correct
ones. Keep it as a sampler that routes cases to the judge and to reviewers, and
measure quality with a judged uniform sample — or, for a specific change, with
an A/B test sized in advance, with guardrail metrics and a stopping rule fixed
before the first look.

## Lab: measure your gate before you trust it {#sec-production-eval-lab}

### Step 1 — build a suite with ground truth you did not label

Fifty to a hundred items, generated from templates with randomised slots, on a
task you care about. The point of generating rather than labelling is that
annotation error cannot contaminate the noise-floor measurement. Keep it in the
repository next to the prompt.

### Step 2 — measure your noise floor

Run the unchanged system over the suite five times and record both the widest
gap and the standard deviation. Do this before writing any gate logic. Write the
`sd` down where the gate's threshold is defined, with the date and the model
version, and set the threshold at roughly four times it. Five runs pin the floor
only loosely — the $\chi^2$ interval on $\sigma$ from four degrees of freedom
puts the true `sd` anywhere from about 0.6 to about 3 times the estimate — so if
the threshold decision is close, run twenty.

### Step 3 — make a regression you would approve in review

Not a deleted rule — that is too easy. Reorder the instructions, or reword one
sentence without changing its meaning. Run it five times. Report the delta as a
multiple of your noise floor, and report per-field or per-category numbers, not
only the aggregate.

### Step 4 — find the mechanism

If the change moved the score, find out *how*. Print the wrong predictions and
look for a pattern; in this chapter every wrong `day` turned out to be the
leading digits of the amount. A regression with a named mechanism becomes a test
case; a regression that is only a number becomes an argument.

### Step 5 — build the gate and measure its false-block rate

Wire the suite into CI so it blocks a merge. Then submit no-op changes and
record how often it blocks them — and pick the count from the precision you
need, because five will not do it: zero blocks out of five still leaves a 95%
Wilson upper bound of **43%**, which cannot distinguish "a few percent" from
"disastrous". Resolving a few-percent rate takes on the order of a hundred
trials, which is cheap when the no-op is a whitespace commit and a scripted
re-run. If the measured rate is above a few percent, your threshold is too
tight — go back to step 2 rather than to the override button.

### Step 6 — run it at temperature 0 as well

Compare reproducibility and score. Confirm whether your per-item results are
identical across runs, and whether the greedy score sits inside or below your
sampled range. Decide deliberately which configuration the gate uses, and write
down why.

### What to hand in

Your measured noise floor with the five run scores behind it; the delta from a
review-invisible edit, as a multiple of that floor, with per-field breakdown; the
mechanism you found for it; your gate's threshold with the reasoning; and its
measured false-block rate, with the number of no-op trials and the 95% Wilson
upper bound. Use enough trials to resolve the rate you need (step 5); five
cannot.

## Exercises {#sec-production-eval-exercises}

1. **Your own noise floor.** Run an unchanged system five times over your real
   eval set. Report the run-to-run `sd` and the widest gap, and compare them to
   the size of the last improvement your team claimed. If the claim is smaller than the floor, say
   what that means.

2. **The invisible edit.** Take a prompt in production and reorder its
   instructions without changing any of them. Run both versions five times.
   Report the delta with per-field numbers, and whether a reviewer could have
   predicted the direction.

3. **Threshold sweep.** Using resampled runs, plot false-block rate and
   catch-rate against threshold for suite sizes 20, 50 and 100. Pick your
   operating point and justify it in one paragraph.

4. **Pairing versus power.** Compute the unpaired sample size needed to resolve
   your measured regression at 80% power (@sec-llm-eval), then compare it to the
   suite size at which your paired gate catches it 95% of the time. Explain the
   gap.

5. **Golden set age.** For each item in your eval set, record when it was added,
   whether it entered as a regression item or a representative one, and whether
   anything has failed it in the last quarter. Retire the representative items
   nothing fails, keep every regression item, and report how many of each are
   left.

6. **Trace to test.** Take three real production complaints, find their traces
   (@sec-observability), and convert each into a suite case. Then check whether
   the original suite contained anything in that failure class.

7. **The three drifts.** Instrument enough to distinguish a model change, an
   input-distribution change and a system change. Then simulate one of each and
   confirm your dashboard tells them apart. Note which evidence you had to
   collect in advance.

8. **Size an A/B test, then peek at it.** Pick a yes/no outcome your system
   logs, and compute the users per arm needed to detect a one-point and a
   two-point change at 80% power (@sec-production-eval-ab), and how many days
   that takes at your traffic. Then simulate an A/A test checked after every
   tenth of the data and report how often it "finds" a difference at p < 0.05.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-production-eval-deeper}

Before reading: run your existing eval suite twice, unchanged, and look at the
two numbers. Whether you can say which differences are real is the whole subject
of this chapter.

This chapter cites no papers, so there is one table rather than the usual two.
The statistical foundations it stands on are in @sec-llm-eval; what follows is
the tooling that turns them into a gate.

## What to remember {#sec-production-eval-summary}

- **A prompt change is a code change, and an eval score is not a unit test.**
  The suite lives in the repository, runs on every prompt change, and blocks the
  merge — but the assertion is statistical, so the gate needs a threshold, and
  the threshold needs a number almost nobody measures.

- **Measure your noise floor; it is a twenty-minute experiment.** Five identical
  runs of the same 100-item suite gave a run-to-run **`sd` of 0.26 points** of
  field accuracy, with an observed range of **0.60**. That is small enough to
  gate on, which contradicts the folklore. Set the threshold from the `sd`
  (about 4 × `sd`), not from the range, which later runs will exceed — and
  without a measured floor no later delta is interpretable.

- **A cosmetic prompt edit is not a cosmetic change.** Reordering six rules with
  nothing added, removed or reworded cost **3.40 points of field accuracy and
  9.20 points of exact match** — about six times the noise floor — and the entire
  regression sat in one field, `day` falling from 91 to 74. [A prompt has no
  interface, so no edit to it is provably local.]{.hl}

- **Report per-field numbers, not only an aggregate.** Across a 40-item probe,
  every wrong `day` under both prompts was the leading digits of the *amount*: the model bleeds one
  field into another, and moving the `amount` rule above the `day` rule tripled
  how often it did. The aggregate showed a wobble; the breakdown showed a
  mechanism, and only a mechanism becomes a test.

- **A gate with no threshold gets worse as your suite grows.** Blocking whenever
  the new score is lower falsely blocked **22.9%** of no-op changes at 20 items
  and **42.5%** at 100, because exact ties vanish and the comparison converges on
  a coin flip. A 1-point threshold at 100 items gives **4.3%** false blocks and
  still catches the reordered prompt **99.4%** of the time.

- **Temperature 0 buys reproducibility, not correctness.** Two runs were
  byte-identical per item — but greedy decoding scored **95.20**, below the whole
  sampled range of 95.40–96.00, and the leading-digit bug was still there. It is
  also a configuration you probably do not serve.

- **The golden set has a lifecycle, and staleness is silent.** It is born from
  real failures, stratified rather than conveniently sampled, and it carries
  personal data. It gets easier as you fix what is in it and the traffic moves
  out from under it, so a set that has not changed in six months is not stable,
  it is stale — and it still produces a green check.

- **Score live traffic in layers.** Free signals on everything — parse rate,
  refusals, latency, tool errors, ceiling hits — then a judge on three
  overlapping samples: a fixed uniform slice, everything that already looks
  wrong, and a stratified slice of the rare. Audit that judge, and pin and record
  its version, because a judge upgrade shifts the whole series.

- **User feedback samples; it does not measure. A/B tests measure, slowly.**
  Thumbs come from a self-selected minority and reward pleasing answers, so use
  them to route cases, not as the score. An A/B test randomises users, fixes one
  primary metric, guardrail metrics and a stopping rule in advance, and is large:
  a one-point change from 20% needs about 24,600 users per arm, and peeking
  daily at ten looks turns a 5% false-positive rate into about 19%.

- **Three drifts look identical on a dashboard.** The model moved, the inputs
  moved, or the system moved — distinguishable only with the responded model and
  the input distribution, both of which must be recorded in advance. Rule out the
  fourth possibility first: that nothing moved and the metric is noisy.
